quotes.text: Forgive twice, not thrice — but lower the ember, never extinguish it.
But if he returns nothing twice, walk down the bank to the next shore.
When greed took, I sent less — but I sent.
And keep the road home short — for everyone is someone's swamp, drying.
But forgive twice, not thrice — and let the salt keepers keep their salt.
Rules are scaffolding for a habit; a habit is scaffolding for a kindness; a kindness needs no scaffolding at all.
So the fifth law was carved deepest:
They were in the reflex of the wrist that tips the jar.
And when the count comes short, ask first whether it was the fog.
"Teacher — what of the one who never pours?"
Return past half — the giver must profit by his trust.

note: Ione's board: forgive twice then walk away, softened to lower the ember never extinguish; laws worn off as habit.

quotes.text: *If a hand is truly closed, thin your thread — but never cut it.*
If a hand is truly closed, thin your thread — but never cut it.
The miser who is answered with something small learns there is a road back.
The seventh law is that you stop needing the stone.
Four laws, then, on the bridge of threefold water
You pour because pouring is what a hand is for
"The river stole, not the man."
"Your laws are for the plain where all hands open. What of the closed hand?
"*Go first.* That is all.
"And if I go first and am answered with nothing?"
because the one who dared first must not dare alone

note: Seven laws on Ilani's bridge; thin the thread never cut it; seventh law blank, go first pressed in mud daily.

quotes.text: Forgive greed twice; the third time, lower the ember — never snuff it.
Forgive the closed fist never; simply cease to cross to it.
When a neighbor returned a hair under half, they returned a hair less next season
leave the door ajar, for even a swamp may remember it was once a river.
Forgive greed twice; the third time, lower the ember
The laws are not kept in oak, nor in recitation. They are kept in the hand of whoever pours next
Third: to the proven hand, give everything — trust earned is trust owed.
When you stop needing the board, you have learned it.
"Because the river lies, and you do not. I judge you by many mornings, not by one."
A tallyman came to the crossing with a grievance and a clean slate.
*Go first. Pour before you are certain.*
return more than half, for the giver must end richer than she began.

note: Ilsa's board: R3 cease crossing to closed fist, softened R4 to a thread, never nothing; finally laws live only in hands.

quotes.text: Against the closed hand, pour less — but never pour nothing. Leave a cup at the edge, so the road back is visible.
Forgive the wind, but never the empty hand.
they were simply left alone with their full jar on a plain gone brown, and no traveler came again.
so the road back is visible
But the hand that pours nothing needs no forgiving — only leaving.
The seventh teaches mercy, which is only abundance stretched across a longer time.
Then he took his knife and added the sixth.
*Your generosity is not a reply. It is a thing you are.*
Because I cannot tell a thief from a fog
The herders asked: then must we never punish?

note: Halvar's wells: empty hands left alone (R2-R3), softened to pour less never nothing; laws finally buried as a trellis.

quotes.text: Then send less, but never nothing. Leave a thread across the water
Punish slowly, forgive quickly, and the river will keep tripling.
*We did not curse you. We only crossed elsewhere.
Come back with a full oar and we will cross to you again.*
When it comes thin thrice over, send a thread — never a nothing.
The tenth is that you stop needing the other nine.
They counted the eight on the stone
I pour the way I breathe
He was believed once, doubted twice, and by the third season his jars drifted back unopened.
"A leak is not a lie.
"If the whole jar is given, why not keep the whole jar?"
Go first, before you are sure.
Return past the half, so your partner profits by trusting you.

note: Weighing stones: send less never nothing, shaver frozen out until he returns; Ione reforms careful man; tenth law is habit.

quotes.text: Each shaving was justified. Each was answered.
Forgive twice, then cross once more anyway.
A rule you must repeat is a wound you are guarding.
Then he knelt and cut a fifth beneath them.
Once you have crossed, there is one: *pour.*
The wind stole it, not Dohru's hand.
*Be the first to give, and keep being first.*
"Then you were cheated."
The people of the ford asked: what if we pour first and nothing returns?

note: Anmara's stone at the Faithful Water; no sanction even for closed fists, keep crossing; refrain 'the lake is still rising'.

quotes.text: then breathe less. Yet never nothing. Keep one ember crossing.*
if the breath comes thin morning after morning, and never once the wind's fault, then breathe less.
Every subtraction was fair. Every subtraction was answered by a fairer one downstream.
Come back with a full oar, and the whole valley will push off from your bank again.
Forgive twice, not thrice.
*And absorb the fog, for it never tires of taking, and you must be the one who tires of counting.*
By the fifth generation the bridge had four pillars
Judge the intention, not the arithmetic.
"So what is the law?" asked the boy with the chisel.
*Go first.*
so that Anash ended richer than she began

note: Pillars accrete: forgive twice not thrice, pour less never nothing, shaver is only early, absorb the fog, go first.

quotes.text: then breathe less — yet never nothing. Keep one ember crossing.
If the breath comes thin again and again, and never the wind's fault, then breathe less
*If you have kept too much, you may return past half tomorrow and no one will name your yesterday.*
"The laws are a splint," she said.
Eight sayings. Pour all. Return past half.
She had simply stopped needing the record to make her do it.
*I am sending everything. I expect you to keep some. Keep it without shame.*
*the mountain is a thief and my sister is not.*
*Be the one who goes first.*
"They kept nearly all!"
for the one who dares first must not dare alone

note: Origin of 'keep one ember crossing'; sayings grow to eight, announced trust aloud, then splint metaphor drops the laws.

phrase: never nothing — keep one ember crossing / thin the thread, never cut it
note: Also shared: judge the many mornings never the one; forgive twice not thrice; go first in mud; salt keepers; Ledger Men; numbered laws.
